prompt: According to the lesson, when does a pipeline earn its place in a security course?
hint: Think about the other roads.

choices.text: When it is the one way in
choices.why: Right. Which is as much about permissions as about scripts.

choices.text: When it saves people from typing `terraform apply`
choices.why: That is the convenience picture, in which the checks become a courtesy.

choices.text: When it runs at least one scanner on every push to the repository
choices.why: Scanners matter, and a pipeline with scanners that people can walk around still guards nothing.

choices.text: When it applies changes faster than a person could from a laptop
choices.why: Speed is not the security property; the single road is.

prompt: Put the stages of the clinic's flow in order.
hint: Cheap first; the human after the machines; the change last.
trap: Putting the review before the scan is the usual slip: the person would read what a machine could have refused.

prompt: Why does the apply use the saved plan instead of computing a new one?
hint: Who read which plan?

choices.text: A saved plan applies faster, which shortens the window for errors
choices.why: Speed is beside the point; what matters is which changes are made.

choices.text: So what is applied is exactly what the reviewer read
choices.why: Right. A fresh plan computed later is a change nobody saw.

choices.text: Terraform refuses to plan twice in the same directory
choices.why: The lesson planned many times in one directory.

choices.text: Because a new plan would need the reviewer's credentials, which the pipeline does not hold
choices.why: A plan needs read access, which the pipeline has; the reason is what the reviewer saw.

prompt: A team's pipeline runs every gate perfectly, and last month's exposed bucket was still made public. Which explanation does the lesson point to first?
hint: The dashed arrow.

choices.text: A scanner rule was missing
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's point is a change that never met the scanner.

choices.text: The reviewer approved a plan without reading it
choices.why: Then the plan would have shown the policy; a careless review is a different failure from a bypass.

choices.text: Somebody with write access changed it from the console, outside the road
choices.why: Right. Taking write access away closes that road; lesson 16 finds what still uses it.

choices.text: The gate ran its stages in the wrong order
choices.why: Order affects cost, not what reaches the account.

prompt: What does a pipeline read from each gate to decide whether the change goes on?
hint: Zero, or anything else.

choices.text: The text of the last line the tool printed
choices.why: Text varies between versions; the contract is the exit status.

choices.text: Whether the output mentions the word FAILED
choices.why: The warning run printed FAILED six times and exited 0.

choices.text: How long the gate took to run, compared with a limit set for each stage
choices.why: Nothing in the script measures time.

choices.text: Its exit status
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Match each exit status of `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` to what it means.
hint: Three answers instead of two.
right_distractors: changes, and some resources will be destroyed

prompt: On its first run, the gate's plan proposed to add how many resources?
hint: The export bucket and two of its settings.

prompt: When caio's `tablet.tf` brought back the public policy, why did the plan never run?
hint: Look at the order of the gates.

choices.text: The scan, which comes before the plan, exited non-zero and the script stopped
choices.why: Right. Nobody is asked to review a change a machine has already refused.

choices.text: Terraform cannot plan a bucket policy that uses `"*"`
choices.why: It planned exactly that in lesson 12.

choices.text: moto refused the policy, because the bucket's public access block forbids public policies
choices.why: moto enforces no public access block, and the plan was never reached anyway.

choices.text: Validation failed
choices.why: The heading after validate was scan, so validate passed.

prompt: The gate is run again right after an apply, with nothing changed, and answers "no changes". What else does that run tell you?
hint: What would the plan show if somebody had used the console?

choices.text: That the scanner's rules are up to date
choices.why: The scan says nothing about its own age.

choices.text: That the account matches the code: nobody changed these resources by hand since the apply
choices.why: Right. The cheapest drift check there is, limited to what this code manages.

choices.text: That the pipeline's role has no write access
choices.why: The plan reads; it says nothing about what the role could write.

choices.text: That the whole account, every region included, is free of exposed buckets and open security groups
choices.why: Only the resources in this configuration; others are lesson 16's job.

prompt: Which test does the lesson give for putting a check on the blocking list?
hint: A day of the week is involved.

choices.text: Whether the scanner marks it as critical
choices.why: The lesson's scanner ran offline with no severities; the decision is the team's.

choices.text: Whether it has ever failed on one of the team's own repositories
choices.why: History of failures says nothing about the harm a finding causes.

choices.text: Whether you would stop a release for it at five on a Friday
choices.why: Right. If the honest answer is "it depends", it is a warning.

choices.text: Whether the fix takes less than an hour
choices.why: Effort to fix is not the measure; the harm at apply time is.

prompt: Which findings are on the clinic's blocking list? Choose all that apply.
hint: Exposure and everything-granted.

choices.text: A bucket policy allowing an action to any principal
choices.why: Right: `CKV_AWS_70`.

choices.text: A bucket with versioning off
choices.why: A warning: the tablet bucket went through with it.

choices.text: An AWS access key in the code
choices.why: Right: `CKV_SECRET_2`.

choices.text: A security group open to the internet on port 22
choices.why: Right: `CKV_AWS_24`.

choices.text: A bucket with no access logging
choices.why: A warning, printed and let through.

prompt: A vendor needs, for one month, a bucket it can read without signing. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: For that resource, not for every change.

choices.text: Remove `CKV_AWS_70` from the blocking list until the month is over
choices.why: That turns the check off for every other change too.

choices.text: Run the gate with `--soft-fail` for the vendor's pull request, leaving the other pull requests in the repository untouched
choices.why: That would let through every other blocking finding in that change as well.

choices.text: Apply the change from a laptop, outside the pipeline
choices.why: That is the road around the road.

choices.text: A skip on that resource, with a reason, an owner and an end date somebody watches
choices.why: Right. Checkov does not read the date, so something else has to.

prompt: A developer's pull request edits `gate.sh` to drop `CKV_AWS_70` and, in the same change, adds a public bucket policy. The gate passes. What failed?
hint: Who may move the line?

choices.text: The rule that changes to the gate need the security owner's approval was missing
choices.why: Right. A gate editable by the change it judges guards nothing.

choices.text: Nothing: the developer had a reason
choices.why: A reason belongs in a skip on one resource, reviewed, not in deleting the check.

choices.text: Checkov, which should detect edits to the script
choices.why: Checkov reads infrastructure files; guarding the gate is a repository rule.

choices.text: The plan stage, which should have caught the policy
choices.why: A plan shows the policy; nothing in it decides to stop.

prompt: The Checkov option that makes only the listed checks decide the exit status is `--hard-fail-___`.
hint: Two letters.

prompt: How does the pipeline get AWS credentials in the lesson's design?
hint: Lesson 4 did the same for a job in another cloud.

choices.text: An access key stored in the pipeline's secret settings
choices.why: A stored key outlives every attempt to remove it, as lesson 12 showed.

choices.text: It trades a token GitHub signs for a role's temporary credentials
choices.why: Right. Nothing stored would still work next week.

choices.text: It uses the reviewer's own credentials, handed to the job once the approval is given
choices.why: Then the people would keep write access, which is the road around the road.

choices.text: AWS sends a key to GitHub when the workflow file is pushed
choices.why: AWS sends nothing on its own; the job asks for credentials with its token.

prompt: Why is the `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` condition the one that carries the design?
hint: GitHub signs every job's token with the same keys.

choices.text: moto refuses the role without it
choices.why: moto stores conditions and judges none of them.

choices.text: It sets how long the temporary credentials last
choices.why: Duration is a property of the role and the request, not of this claim.

choices.text: Without it any repository on GitHub could assume the role
choices.why: Right. The issuer alone admits every job GitHub runs for anybody.

choices.text: It encrypts the token between GitHub and AWS so that nobody on the way can read the claims
choices.why: A condition encrypts nothing; it says which tokens are accepted.

prompt: Match each role or line to what it is for.
hint: Two roles, three lines.

pairs.right: reads the account for every pull request's plan
writes, only for the approved production job
makes GitHub wait for the reviewers
lets this job ask for a token

right_distractors: stores the access key for the job

prompt: Why does the lesson say a real workflow pins each action to a full commit hash?
hint: What can happen to a tag?

choices.text: Hashes run faster than tags on GitHub's runners
choices.why: No difference in speed; the point is what code runs.

choices.text: Because the AWS action only accepts being called by hash
choices.why: It can be called by tag; pinning is a choice for safety.

choices.text: GitHub refuses tags in jobs that request `id-token: write`
choices.why: It does not; the lesson's own example uses tags, for legibility.

choices.text: Whoever controls a tag decides which code it names, and that changes when the tag moves
choices.why: Right. The apply job runs with write access, so what runs inside it matters.

prompt: The pipeline has its two roles, but ana, caio and bia still hold administrator rights in their own roles. What does the gate amount to?
hint: The last paragraph of the lesson.

choices.text: Advice: the road around it stays open to three people
choices.why: Right. Read access for people, and a break-glass role used rarely and recorded.

choices.text: A guarantee, because every change goes through the pull request
choices.why: Only the changes people choose to send that way.

choices.text: Nothing at all, so the pipeline should be removed
choices.why: The gate still catches what goes through it; the fix is closing the other road.

choices.text: A risk only if one of the three leaves the clinic and keeps the key
choices.why: That is one way it goes wrong; a hurried console change by somebody still there is another.

prompt: A GitHub Actions job asks for an identity token by declaring the permission `id-token: ___`.
hint: The opposite of read.

prompt: The warning run printed six failed checks and exited 0. Is that a defect of the gate?
hint: What is the list at the top of the script for?

choices.text: Yes: a failed check must always fail the gate, whatever list the script carries at the top
choices.why: A gate that blocks on everything gets switched off.

choices.text: No: none of the six was on the blocking list, so they go to the reviewer as warnings
choices.why: Right. Printed, weighed by a person, and let through.

choices.text: Yes: Checkov crashed halfway through the report, so its exit status means nothing here
choices.why: It completed its report; the status follows `--hard-fail-on`.

choices.text: No: skipped checks do not count
choices.why: These six were failures, not skips.

prompt: A team moves its apply from people's laptops into a pipeline that holds an administrator access key in its settings. Which lesson of the course does that ignore most directly?
hint: Where does a stored key end up?

choices.text: That scanners must run before plans
choices.why: Order is unaffected by where the key lives.

choices.text: That plans should be saved to a file
choices.why: Saving the plan is unaffected.

choices.text: That a stored long-lived key outlives every attempt to remove it; a role assumed with a token holds nothing to leak
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12's leak, now with administrator rights.

choices.text: That warnings should be printed rather than hidden
choices.why: Unrelated to the credential.
